Turn this into a closed question:
What are Countable and Uncountable Nouns?
cannot be separated into individual elements:
on what's countable! This can cause mistakes like:
a) I don’t have ___ time right now.
b) She bought ___ bananas and ___ rice.
c) I need ___ advice. Can you help?
b) I have a lot of information.
He gave me many good advices.
4. Fill in with ‘much’, ‘many’, or ‘a lot of’:
There isn’t ___ sugar left, but there are ___ cookies.
furniture, luggage, hair (on head), traffic, jewelry.
Can you give me an advice?
You mean "some advice"! Advice is uncountable.
How many homeworks do we have?
We don’t say “homeworks.” Just “some homework” or “a lot of homework.”
If you mean the hair on her head, say “a lot of hair.” "Hairs" usually means individual strands.
It was Lucas’s first day at the new company. He brought all his equipments, prepared with a list of informations he had researched. His supervisor smiled and said,
“You’re ready—but remember, we say ‘equipment’ and ‘information’ without ‘s’ in English.”
Later, Lucas asked for an advice. The supervisor replied,
“Just ask! ‘Advice’ is uncountable—so you can ask for some advice, not an advice.”
Lucas laughed, realizing Portuguese and English don't always agree on what can be counted!
What were Lucas's mistakes with uncountable nouns?
How did his supervisor correct him?
What’s the main point of the story?
a) She gave me a great advice.
b) We bought two new furnitures.
c) I found many interesting informations online.
He gave me many good advices about career choices.
a) Você tem alguma informação sobre o projeto?
b) Eu preciso de um conselho.
c) Compramos dois móveis novos para a sala.
A: Did you bring all the equipment?
A: And what about the advice he gave?
don’t use a/an or plural s
"Three pieces of advice I’ve received in my life."
